snippet.title: Angkor Wat: The Lost Megacity Hidden in the Jungle (AI Reconstruction)
snippet.description:
Basically, in this video, I use modern AI to reconstruct Angkor Wat at its absolute peak—before the droughts, floods, and its eventual collapse. We travel back to the year 1296 to walk through the world's greatest hydraulic city, exactly as it was. It’s not just about looking at buildings; we explore the daily life of its 750,000 inhabitants through the accounts of Zhou Daguan, the only surviving first-person eyewitness to document it. We contrast that vibrant reality—central towers blazing with gold leaf and bustling markets run entirely by female merchants—with the silent, jungle-swallowed ruins revealed by modern LIDAR technology today.

We also break down the exact moment the climate turned chaotic, bringing decades of severe drought followed by extreme monsoons. It’s crazy to see how the very water and sophisticated engineering system that sustained this massive pre-industrial civilization for 500 years ultimately destroyed it.

snippet.title: Experience a Week in Ancient Egypt | Day 7: The Festival of Opet (Series Finale)
snippet.description:
For six days, you've lived six different lives in ancient Egypt.

You've carried mud bricks as a farmer. Carved a god's face into stone as a tomb builder. Dressed a golden statue before dawn as a priest. Negotiated deals in a market without money as an Egyptian wife. Survived a desert battle as a soldier. Sat with a grieving husband as a physician.

Today, on Day 7, all of them are in the same crowd.

This is the Festival of Opet — the largest religious gathering in the ancient world. Once a year, the entire city of Thebes stops working. Every farmer, every stonemason, every priest, every merchant, every soldier home on leave converges on the same street to watch the most powerful deity in the Egyptian universe carried through the city in a golden boat.

Today the city feeds you for free. Today the social rules briefly relax. Today a priest who has spent a month alone in a dark room finally steps out into sunlight. Today a soldier who killed a man in the desert drinks wine and watches the stars and is, for one quiet hour, almost at peace.

Today six lives become one crowd. One city. One shared moment in 1250 BC.

Using AI trained on the actual Opet Festival inscriptions carved into the walls of Luxor Temple — inscriptions that still survive today — we've reconstructed what the greatest festival of the ancient world actually looked like.

snippet.title: How 300 Spartans Brutally Stopped Persia's Largest Army (Thermopylae, 480 BC)
snippet.description:
In 480 BC, the largest invasion army in ancient history marched toward Greece — and 300 Spartans under King Leonidas stood in their way at Thermopylae. This is the documented military history of how a few thousand Greek hoplites, fighting in the phalanx formation, held off the entire Persian Empire for three days in a narrow pass called the Hot Gates. Not the Zack Snyder version. The real story — researched from primary sources and reconstructed frame by frame as an AI ancient history documentary.
Three weeks before the battle, King Leonidas walked into the Oracle at Delphi and was told either Sparta would fall, or a Spartan king must die. He chose 300 Spartans — not the strongest, not the fastest — but men who already had living sons to carry their names forward. Every man he picked understood, without being told, what that selection meant. By the time Leonidas reached the Hot Gates, his force of 300 Spartans and several thousand Greek allies stood between the entire Persian Empire and the rest of the ancient world.
In this video, we rebuild the three days that changed Western civilization — the Persian war machine of Xerxes, the genius geography of the Hot Gates, the wall of bronze shields that broke the Immortals, the betrayal of Ephialtes, and the final stand on the hill where the line that had never broken finally did. This is the real story of King Leonidas, the 300 Spartans, and the Battle of Thermopylae — the documented history of the men who chose to die in a corridor of rock and salt water so that Greece, and the civilisation that grew out of it, could survive.

🎬 HOW WE MAKE THESE VIDEOS — RESEARCH, AI RECONSTRUCTION, CAPCUT
At Worlds Before Us, every video starts with deep historical research — primary ancient sources, leading modern scholars, archaeological records, museum archives. We do not skim Wikipedia. We read the actual books. Once the script is locked, we use modern AI image and video generation tools to visually reconstruct moments no camera was ever there to capture — every frame generated from period-accurate references like surviving 5th-century-BCE Greek hoplite armour, the actual Thermopylae geography as it would have appeared before two millennia of coastal silting, contemporary Persian military equipment, and primary-source descriptions of phalanx warfare. The final edit is assembled in CapCut, where we layer the AI-generated visuals with cinematic sound design, narration, and pacing built specifically for retention. The result lets you see, not just hear, what it actually looked like to stand in that corridor. We do not invent — we reconstruct, frame by frame, from the historical record.

📚 HISTORICAL SOURCES USED FOR THIS SCRIPT
The script for this video draws on the following ancient and modern works for its claims about the Battle of Thermopylae, the 300 Spartans, Leonidas's selection criteria, Xerxes' invasion, and the events of August 480 BCE:
• Herodotus — The Histories, Books VII–VIII (c. 430 BCE). The primary ancient source for the Greco-Persian Wars, written within a generation of the events depicted. The detail about Leonidas selecting men with living sons appears in Book VII, 205.
• Tom Holland — Persian Fire: The First World Empire and the Battle for the West (Little, Brown, 2005). The definitive modern narrative history of the Greco-Persian Wars, covering Xerxes' invasion and Thermopylae in detail.
• Paul Cartledge — Thermopylae: The Battle That Changed the World (Overlook Press, 2006). The standard academic monograph on the battle by the leading modern Spartan historian.
• Victor Davis Hanson — The Western Way of War: Infantry Battle in Classical Greece (University of California Press, 1989) and Carnage and Culture (Doubleday, 2001). Sources on Greek hoplite tactics, the phalanx formation, and the mechanics of the rotation system used at Thermopylae.
• Peter Green — The Greco-Persian Wars (University of California Press, 1996). Authoritative scholarly survey of the entire conflict.
• Plutarch — Apophthegmata Laconica (Sayings of the Spartans). Source for the "molon labe" exchange and other Spartan-attributed quotes.
• Diodorus Siculus — Bibliotheca Historica, Book XI (c. 60–30 BCE). Alternate ancient account of the battle.
• Barry Strauss — The Battle of Salamis: The Naval Encounter That Saved Greece — and Western Civilization (Simon & Schuster, 2004). Source for the strategic context immediately before and after Thermopylae.

snippet.description:
Basically, in this video, we reconstruct the most extraordinary eighty years in the life of Athens. We explore how the city rose from a burnt-out shell left by the Persians to become the greatest naval empire the ancient Mediterranean had ever seen. It's not just about looking at pristine white marble; we explore how a cracked, cruel, brilliant democracy built the Parthenon using allied defense money , contrasting the violent blues, blood reds, and sweating marble gods of the Acropolis with the hellish reality of the Laurium silver mines. Down there, thousands of slaves were worked to a waxy death in oven-like temperatures to fund the empire's reserve currency. 

We also break down the terrifying machine of Athenian justice , the devastating plague that wiped out a third of the city's population , and how the citizens voted, one assembly at a time, to hand their city over to its enemies. It's crazy to see how the same people who built a wooden wall of ships to save Western civilization ultimately built a wall of fear high enough to execute their own victorious generals , vote to massacre neutral islands like Melos , and force Socrates to drink hemlock. Sparta didn't conquer Athens; Athens conquered itself.

snippet.title: You Wouldn't Survive 24 Hours on a Viking Longship, 900 AD
snippet.description:
No cabin. No toilet. No shelter. Thirty-two men on a twenty-three-meter wooden ship crossing the North Atlantic with nothing between them and the ocean but oak planks held together with iron rivets. The hull is so thin you can feel the waves through the wood with your hand.
 
Sleep comes in fragments of one to three hours on a wet deck. Food is dried fish eaten cold because fire on a wooden ship is suicide. The toilet is the side of the ship, which in rough seas means removing your clothes in freezing wind a meter above the water. And the navigator carries every route in his memory — no maps, no compass, no charts. If he dies, the ship is lost.
 
This is the vehicle that discovered North America five hundred years before Columbus. This is what 24 hours on a Viking longship actually looked like.

snippet.title: What Was It Like Being A Monk During the Black Death? | Medieval London 1348 | Day 2 of 7
snippet.description:
Forty percent of England's clergy were dead by the end of 1349.

Not fled. Not retired. Dead. The monks and priests who went into the infected houses — who held the hands of the dying, administered last rites, heard confessions in rooms where every breath was a risk — died at twice the rate of the general population. The people most obligated to stay were the people most likely to die for staying.

This is Day 2 of our 7-part series: A Week in Medieval London.

Today, you are a Benedictine monk at Westminster Abbey, November 1348. You wake up at two in the morning for Matins. You pray seven times a day, every day, without exception. You tend to the dying in the infirmary with treatments you suspect are not working. You sit beside a brother who has been here for twenty years and sing psalms with him while he is still able to move his lips.

And this afternoon, a letter arrives from the Bishop of London that has never been sent before in the history of the English church — because there are simply not enough priests left to do what priests are supposed to do.

The Rule of Saint Benedict was written for exactly this. For the moments when everything wants you to stop, go quiet, and retreat into private grief. The Rule says: get up. Say the office. Come back tomorrow.

Using AI trained on monastic records, medieval chronicles, and the actual canonical hours of Benedictine life, we've reconstructed what one day inside Westminster Abbey actually looked like in November 1348.

snippet.title: Why This Aviation Disaster Still Haunts Experts | AI Reconstruction Tenerife, 1977
snippet.description:
On March 27, 1977, 583 people died when two Boeing 747s collided on a foggy runway in Tenerife. It remains the deadliest accident in aviation history.

The pilot who caused it was not inexperienced. He was KLM's chief flight instructor, responsible for training every 747 pilot in the airline. His face appeared in their advertisements. When KLM heard about the crash, they called him to lead the investigation — then realized he was in the plane.

Arthur Graves uses advanced AI reconstruction to walk through the chain of errors that led to the disaster: a bomb that hurt no one, a refueling that blocked an exit, a fog that blinded everyone, and three seconds of radio static that erased the only two messages that could have stopped everything.

Every safety procedure you rely on when you fly was written because of what happened here.

Basically, in this video, I use AI to "resurrect" Kyiv — the Viking capital of the Slavic world — and walk its streets exactly as they were around 1050 AD, right before the empire it built began to fracture from within. It's not just about looking at buildings; we explore the massive slave-trading docks of the Podol, the golden domes of Saint Sophia rising above the Dnieper, and the ceremonial Golden Gate at the absolute peak of their power. snippet.title: Why You Wouldn't Survive a Medieval Oubliette: The Punishment Worse Than Death in 1475
snippet.description:
How did a medieval French punishment exist that contemporaries openly called worse than death?

Autumn 1475. Château de Loches, France. A prisoner is lowered through a hole in a stone floor into a pit with no door, no stairs, no name — and a word designed for what it was meant to do. Oubliette. From the French verb "to forget." He has not been sentenced to die. He has been sentenced to be forgotten.

Under Louis XI — the king his contemporaries called "the Universal Spider" — long-term confinement became a formal tool of statecraft. His most famous prisoner at Loches was Cardinal Jean Balue, his own former chief minister, held in an iron cage for eleven years before Pope Sixtus IV personally intervened to free him in 1480. The cages were nicknamed les fillettes du roi — "the king's little daughters." The cheaper variant beneath the cage was the oubliette — the pit used when the king did not need a prisoner remembered, only erased.

In this AI Reconstruction we rebuild what 1475 inside the Loches oubliette actually looked like. The bottle-dungeon shape — wider at the base, narrowing toward the iron grate above. The conical sloped floor that pulled the prisoner toward the centre and would not let him lie flat. The drip-feed of bread through the grate — kept alive, just barely, for months. The water sluice that flooded the cell with cold moat water up to his ankles, his shins, his knees. The rats that came up from the foundation drains. The hallucinations that began after three weeks of total isolation. And the documented medieval thesis: this punishment was worse than execution because death gave you a body, a name in a parish register, a witness. The oubliette gave you none.

And here is what nobody tells you. Most "oubliettes" shown to tourists in European castles today are not oubliettes. The shaft at Warwick Castle long advertised as a medieval prison-pit has been re-examined by modern archaeologists and is almost certainly a latrine. Most of the Gothic image of medieval Europe came from Walter Scott and Victor Hugo, not from the medieval record itself.

But the real ones existed. At Loches the carceral architecture is documented and real — preserved spaces in the Tour Ronde and the Martelet consistent with the design described in 15th-century chronicles. Pierrefonds. Plessis-lès-Tours. Certain Italian fortezze. Purpose-built pits with no side entrance, only a ceiling oculus, sloped floors, and a single sluice gate operated from above.

Our prisoner at Loches in autumn 1475 is in one of the real ones. His name was never written again. That, in the end, was the point.

Every claim is sourced from Philippe de Commynes (Louis XI's own chronicler), Paul Murray Kendall's modern scholarship on Louis XI, the Loches archaeological record, and 15th-century French chronicle tradition. snippet.title: Marathon — The Day a Democracy Beat an Empire
snippet.description:
In 490 BC, a democracy barely eighteen years old marched out to face the largest empire on earth — outnumbered, almost alone, on open ground that favored the enemy. By nightfall, Athens had done what
the world believed impossible. It had beaten Persia.

This is the first Persian invasion of Greece — the warning before Xerxes, ten years before Thermopylae and Salamis. Athens had helped Greek cities rebel against Persia, and King Darius sent a fleet to punish it. The Persians landed on a coastal plain north of the city, a place called Marathon.

This episode breaks down the battle tactically: why the Athenians chose the suicidal gamble of fighting in the open, why Sparta arrived too late, and the masterpiece of the general Miltiades — a deliberately thin center and crushing wings that became a double envelopment. The same deadly idea Hannibal would perfect at Cannae nearly three centuries later was already used here, in 490 BC, to break a Persian army.

And it separates the legend from the history: the true origin of the marathon race, the lone runner of myth versus the entire army that force-marched twenty-six miles home to save its city, and why this single afternoon may have saved the golden age of Athens — and the West that grew from it.

snippet.title: Medieval London 1348 | A Day in the Life of an Grave Digger (Black Death) | day 4 of 7
snippet.description:
When archaeologists excavated East Smithfield in London in 1986, they found something unexpected.

The bodies weren't buried randomly. They were laid out in neat rows — perfectly aligned, hands folded, shrouded where possible. Over ten thousand of them. In less than two years.

Somebody did that work. Thousands of times. In November mud. For very little pay. And nobody ever wrote their name down.

This is Day 4 of our 7-part series: A Week in Medieval London.

Today, you are a gravedigger at East Smithfield — the emergency burial ground the Bishop of London consecrated in November 1348 because the parish churchyards were already full. You sleep in a lean-to shelter at the edge of the site. You eat dark bread before dawn. You dig trenches alongside a man named Walter who has made a private agreement with himself about what this job is and is not, and who has not shared the terms of that agreement with anyone.

The carts come every morning. You lay the bodies in rows, east to west, the way the Christian tradition requires — so that when they rise at the Last Judgement they will face Jerusalem. You fold their hands where folding is possible. You do this thirty times today.

One of them is a child wrapped in a blue wool blanket with an embroidered flower near the corner. Someone sewed that flower on an ordinary day that was not this day.

You notice it. You don't mention it to Walter. You go back to the digging.

Using AI trained on the Museum of London's excavation reports and medieval city records, we've reconstructed what one day as a gravedigger at East Smithfield actually looked like in November 1348.

snippet.title: What It Was Like to Survive 1816, the Year Without Summer (AIReconstruction)
snippet.description:
What if one volcano on the other side of the world could kill summer for an entire
year — and accidentally create Frankenstein?
Lake Geneva. June 1816. An eighteen-year-old woman named Mary Godwin sits at a desk
in Villa Diodati with a candle burning at noon. The fire is lit. The lake outside is
grey. The rain has not stopped for four weeks. Mary has not seen the sun in nine
days. It is June. It should not be like this.
Eight thousand kilometres away, on the morning of the fifth of April eighteen fifteen,
a mountain in Indonesia called Tambora exploded with the most powerful blast humans
have recorded in the last ten thousand years. A VEI-7 eruption. Four times the ejecta
of Krakatoa. Sir Stamford Raffles, the British Lieutenant-Governor of Java, recorded
the explosions in his official journal that night.
Within a single week, at least seventy-one thousand people were dead. An entire
Indonesian kingdom — the Sultanate of Tambora — ceased to exist. Its language was
spoken by no one alive when the ash cleared. A vocabulary, a culture, an entire small
civilisation, erased in seven days.
But the death toll on the island was not what would matter most. What would matter
most was something the survivors could not see. Somewhere between ten and one hundred
and twenty million tonnes of sulfur dioxide had been blown forty kilometres into the
stratosphere, where it formed a sulfuric acid veil that wrapped the entire planet.
A year later, in 1816, the veil reached its peak.
In Sharon, Vermont, a farmer named Solomon Putnam watched snow fall on his cornfield
on the eighth of June. In Württemberg, Germany, families packed everything they owned
and started walking east toward Russia — a migration historians later called "the
Walking Country." In England, mobs of starving labourers smashed bakery windows in
what the press called the Bread or Blood riots. In Ireland, the typhus epidemic that
followed the famine killed an estimated one hundred thousand people. In Germany, a
young engineer named Karl Drais invented the modern bicycle — because so many horses
had starved to death that Europe needed a new way to travel.
And at the Villa Diodati, four people trapped indoors by impossible cold invented the
modern horror story. Mary Godwin wrote Frankenstein. John Polidori wrote The Vampyre
— the literary grandfather of Dracula. Lord Byron wrote "Darkness," the apocalyptic
poem still read at every climate conference today.
In this AI Reconstruction we rebuild what 1816 actually looked like. The lightning
over Lake Geneva. The snow on Vermont cornfields. The German families walking east.
The Irish typhus wards. The Protestant preachers across the world declaring the end
times had begun. And the one volcano in Indonesia that started all of it.
This is not a story about a bad summer. This is a story about how one geological
event eight thousand kilometres away rewrote European literature, killed at least
ninety thousand people across three continents, invented a vehicle, and convinced an
entire generation that the world was ending.

snippet.title: Birmingham 1900: The City That Promised Paradise
snippet.description:
Basically, in this video, I use AI to "resurrect" Birmingham—the red-brick city that armed the British Empire—and walk its streets exactly as they were between 1890 and 1929, at the absolute peak of its industrial power. It's not just about looking at factories; we explore the Jewellery Quarter where seventy thousand craftsmen made more than half the jewelry in the entire Empire, the BSA arms works that produced 1.5 million rifles for a single war, and the monumental Council House of a city that declared itself the best-governed on earth—at their absolute peak. We contrast that vibrant reality—the cleanest mountain water on the British mainland, the first municipal bank in the country, the oldest cinema still standing in Britain—with the one hundred and eight thousand toxic back-to-back houses where its workers slept under the same yellow smoke that built the Empire.

We also break down the real story the world never got right: who the actual Peaky Blinders were—teenage boys with belt buckles and bad luck, not razor blades sewn into caps—how the most liberal democracy on earth built an industrial torture system inside its own model prison to force-feed women asking to vote, and how Birmingham armed an entire world war while sending its own sons to die with the weapons their wives and mothers had just forged. It's crazy to see what this city sacrificed to keep an empire running, especially since—unlike every other lost city we've rebuilt on this channel, destroyed by fire, water, armies, or plague—Birmingham was suffocated by the one thing it refused to admit: the same red brick that built the Empire was choking the people inside it.
